# Tracking of all of the things that Yuhong would like updates on:

## Tracking evals
How are the evaluations going for updating documents to the wiki? Place updates as bullet points below

How is the evaluation for agents updating the documents going? I want updates as bullet points below

- PR 79 adds an offline `backend/evals/` suite for wiki-reading and wiki-writing agents, kept outside `tests/` because live runs hit real LLMs and are parameterized by `(provider, model)`.
- v0 coverage includes 30 `wiki_updater` cases across `NO_CHANGE` / `CHANGE` / `IRRELEVANT`, bloat-bait, and loss-bait scenarios, plus 5 `ingest_selector` cases and 24 external-agent scenarios. The suite evaluates both **WHEN** to trigger and **HOW** good the output is.
- Scorers include deterministic checks such as `trigger_class_match`, `bloat_ratio`, `markdown_valid`, and `selector_set_metrics`, plus LLM judges for `facts_present` and `facts_preserved`.
- CI now has `evals-smoke.yml` for PR dry-runs plus eval unit tests, and `evals-nightly.yml` for live matrix runs that push to Braintrust.
- The 2026-05-22 live full matrix completed for `ingest_selector`, `wiki_updater.process_instruction`, `wiki_updater.reconcile_document`, and `external_agent`, and all four runs pushed to Braintrust. Headline results: `gpt-5-mini` leads `ingest_selector` F1 at 0.92 vs. `claude-haiku-4-5` at 0.58; `claude-sonnet-4-6` has perfect `process_instruction` trigger macro F1 and external-agent update routing; `gpt-5` and Sonnet are roughly tied on ingest reconciliation, with both preserving existing facts.
- PR 93 adds opt-in real-traffic eval logging at the ingest reconciler stage. When `INGEST_EVAL_LOGGING=true`, reconciler decisions are written to a new `ingest_eval_samples` table with the source document, wiki page before reconciliation, unified diff, outcome (`committed`/`no_change`), and commit SHA; logging is off by default and does not run for BM25 or selector stages. The Helm chart publishes this env var starting in chart `0.3.18`, and dev-wiki worker pods set `INGEST_EVAL_LOGGING=true`. `backend/scripts/eval_labeler.html` is a self-contained offline browser tool for labeling exported `ingest_eval_samples` JSONL rows with six granular outcomes: **Should commit — critical**, **Should commit — moderate**, **Should commit — nit**, **Should no-change — already covered**, **Should no-change — extra info, not worth inclusion**, and **Should be irrelevant — wrong selection**. Should-commit labels require a note describing what the update should cover. The tool stores labels, coverage notes, `source_summary` / `wiki_summary` / `diff_summary`, and `judge_label` / `judge_reasoning` fields inline on each row and writes them back to the original `.jsonl` file via the File System Access API. Summaries are generated manually per sample through Anthropic in the browser; matching source/wiki summaries are propagated to rows with identical content, and the Anthropic key is kept only in memory for the current tab. The Judge button, also available with the `j` key, asks `claude-opus-4-7` for an independent suggestion using only the source document and wiki page, not the diff or outcome; the suggestion appears as a yellow label-card box for human confirmation or override. Judge results propagate to rows with identical source and wiki content, and the judge prompt penalizes detail dumps that exceed wiki scope, defaulting to the extra-info no-change label when unsure. Exporting `ingest_eval_samples` JSONL rows is handled by `ods` operational tooling.
- PR 99 tightens the ingest batch reconciler prompt against edit-level bloat: wiki pages are framed as current truth for a reader looking up one fact, external docs are treated as often longer than wiki pages, and `replace` text should stay as short as the corrected/new fact allows. Test plan is to run `evals-nightly.yml` on bloat cases and compare `bloat_ratio` for `reconcile_document` against the v0 baseline (~0.88–0.92), plus manually inspect long-doc outputs.
- PR 110 adds a Scope check to the ingest reconciler prompt between relevance and editing rules: the wiki page's existing purpose, structure, and granularity determine whether related source-document details belong, and `no_change` is the tiebreaker when fit is unclear.
- PR 108 extends `backend/evals/README.md` with a scorer reference for all 13 scorers, Braintrust experiment-reading guidance, and contributor how-tos for adding cases, adding surfaces, and debugging failed trials. The Braintrust guide prioritizes `error_rate`, then `trigger.macro_f1`, then `facts_preserved < 0.9` as a silent-degradation signal; nightly eval cost is documented at roughly $15–25 per run.

## Tracking UX
How is progress on the deploying Agents via the UI? I want to know when it can support claude code, craft, etc.

- The Custom Agents docs now describe Agents as reusable AI team members for specific tasks that can be used individually or shared with users/user-groups in Onyx. The Agent creation flow includes natural-language Instructions, scoped Knowledge from Connectors or file uploads, and Actions; connector-backed knowledge is kept up to date as external documents change.
- The Agent Wiki SetupWizard "Set up tools" step 2 Install Helper pane now stacks the Download installer button above the helper text so the CTA label and helper paragraph wrap cleanly at narrow widths.
- PR 103 migrates Agent Wiki buttons and nav icons across all pages to OPAL v2 components, removes the legacy `src/components/common/Button.tsx` shim, and adopts Hanken Grotesk for sans-serif text and DM Mono for code-style text via `next/font/google`. The font variables are applied on `<html>` in `layout.tsx`, with DM Mono wired to `code`, `pre`, `kbd`, and `samp` in `globals.css`.
- A Discord question flags that the expected update behavior for the File Connector needs clarification: whether it can detect file changes over time automatically, or whether users must re-upload the file every time it changes.
- A Discord question asks whether Onyx can link directly to a NAS directory path instead of requiring manual `.zip` uploads. The supported path for NAS/directory-based ingestion, if any, still needs clarification. Current File Connector guidance says bundling files into a `.zip` is the supported and recommended method for bulk uploads. Very large individual files can cause memory issues during processing even without a hard hard limit, so self-hosted deployments should set reasonable `MAX_FILE_SIZE_BYTES` values as a safety net; on Onyx Cloud, these environment variables are managed by the Onyx backend, so teams should contact Onyx if they hit large-file processing issues.
- A Discord clarification for the upload error `Some files were not uploaded. Document contains too many embedded images.` says Onyx caps embedded images to prevent memory overloads. Defaults are 500 embedded images per file and 1,000 embedded images per upload batch; users should reduce/compress images or split PDFs into smaller parts. For ZIP uploads, files over the cap are skipped and warnings identify rejected files. Self-hosted admins can adjust `MAX_EMBEDDED_IMAGES_PER_FILE` and `MAX_EMBEDDED_IMAGES_PER_UPLOAD`.
- The GitHub connector has an optional `include_files` / “Include Documents?” setting for indexing human-readable repository files from the default branch. It indexes `.md`, `.mdx`, `.markdown`, `.rst`, `.txt`, and common extensionless docs such as README and LICENSE files; skips denylisted paths such as `.git` and `node_modules`, files over 1 MB, and non-text or undecodable content; and requires at least one of PRs, issues, or files to be enabled. The files stage checkpoints pagination in 100-file batches, uses `pushed_at` to skip unchanged repos, emits blob links/file-based identifiers/hierarchy metadata, and surfaces truncated repository trees as failures. GitHub 404s for disabled PR or issue endpoints skip those stages instead of failing, and FILES pagination resumes without stage regression so each file is indexed once.
- The Custom Agents docs also describe an Admin Panel Agents page where admins can create new Agents, edit configurations, designate featured Agents, hide/show or delete Agents, attach knowledge sources, add Actions, configure model/knowledge options, and publish Agents to the organization or to specific users/groups. Built-in Actions such as Internal Search, Web Search, and Image Generation require setup in the admin panel before use; Code Execution is listed as a built-in Action that does not require configuration. The docs do not mention Claude Code or Craft support.
- A Craft PR improves scheduled task reliability by waking or creating the user's sandbox when a scheduled task fires. The executor now calls `SessionManager.ensure_sandbox_running` headlessly for SLEEPING, TERMINATED, FAILED, missing, or unhealthy RUNNING sandbox cases; it waits up to 120 seconds for concurrent PROVISIONING to finish and honors org concurrency limits in `MULTI_TENANT`. This should prevent scheduled runs from silently skipping just because the user closed Craft and the sandbox went to sleep. Prior in-flight provisioning is now the only skip path; provisioning timeouts or other wake failures mark the run FAILED with `error_class=sandbox_wake_failed` and send a scheduled-task failure notification. Scheduled-task outcomes now use explicit `ScheduledTaskErrorClass` and `ScheduledTaskSkipReason` enums, with exception class and message captured in `error_detail`.
- A Craft PR refactors built-in skills so they are seeded as tenant `skill` table rows with a nullable `built_in_skill_id` discriminator; this is now the preferred way to reference built-ins instead of the old in-memory registry. The migration seeds `pptx`, `image-generation`, and `company-search` rows idempotently for existing tenants, makes bundle source columns nullable behind an XOR check, and treats migrations as the source of truth: there is no boot-time seeding or runtime metadata refresh. The migration also drops the legacy orphan `skill.manifest_metadata` column with `DROP COLUMN IF EXISTS` before the built-in seed so existing tenants that still have the old NOT NULL column migrate successfully. The change should make built-ins flow through normal DB-backed listing, permission, fileset, and `AGENTS.md` generation paths while keeping them immutable: admin mutations are rejected, they are not group-shareable, and unavailable or unknown built-ins are hidden or skipped. Fileset/`AGENTS.md` generation now reads built-ins from disk, renders `company-search` per user, and bundle validation rejects reserved built-in slugs.
- Craft Kubernetes sandboxes can deliver built-in skills through an S3 Files skills backend when `SKILLS_S3_BUCKET` is set. api_server mirrors built-ins to S3 best-effort at startup, and sandbox pods mount an `efs.csi.aws.com` volume read-only at `/skills/` using a per-tenant access point; in-pod setup symlinks `.agents/skills/<slug>` to `/skills/_builtins/<slug>`. The backend is disabled when `SKILLS_S3_BUCKET` is unset, so local/dev and docker-compose behavior stays unchanged. Additional configuration includes `SKILLS_S3_PREFIX` and `SKILLS_S3_FILES_FILE_SYSTEM_ID`.
- Commonly useful public skills and memories should live in the repo when they can be public. Private shared skills and memories live in the `onyx-llm-context` repo; `ods install-skill` installs skills from that repo. `ods` v0.7.8 uses Bun instead of npm for its internal package-manager calls, so local and CI workflows that run `ods` need Bun installed.
- A Craft PR removes the unsupported `public_global` sharing scope, which was never surfaced in the Craft UI. Craft webapp access now always requires an authenticated user, and frontend sharing options are narrowed to `private` and `public_org`; tests now cover private owner-only access and public-org access for non-owner org members. The webapp proxy route stays on `public_build_router` so unauthenticated browser visits still get the friendly 401-to-302 redirect to `/auth/login`.
- A Craft PR hardens the sandbox webapp proxy by stripping viewer credentials and identity headers before forwarding requests to the sandbox Next.js server. The proxy now deny-lists cookies, `Authorization`, `X-Api-Key`, CSRF tokens, hop-by-hop headers, `Forwarded`/`X-Forwarded-*`, IDP headers, `Host`, `Content-Length`, and any header beginning with `x-onyx-`; only benign headers needed by Next.js, such as `Accept` and `User-Agent`, should pass through. The PR notes this has no functional impact because the sandbox webapp is a frontend-only Next.js shell with no callbacks into Onyx, and tests assert sensitive headers are stripped case-insensitively.
- A Craft PR removes generated `sessions/$session_id/org_info/` content from both local and Kubernetes sandbox managers. New sandbox workspaces should no longer include `user_identity_profile.txt`, `organization_structure.json`, or an `org_info/AGENTS.md`, and generated `AGENTS.md` files no longer include the Organization Info section. The refactor also deletes the old persona-mapping path and removes `user_work_area` / `user_level` plumbing from session creation because those fields were only used for org-info setup.
- A Craft PR speeds up sandbox session setup by replacing per-session `npm install` with `bun install --frozen-lockfile --backend=hardlink` against a pod-wide Bun tarball cache. Warm new sessions on an existing pod drop from about 12.07s to 0.40s, cold new sessions from about 27.99s to 15.99s, and per-session `node_modules` disk overhead drops from about 840 MB to about 20 MB because files hardlink back to the shared cache. Snapshots now exclude `outputs/web/node_modules` and `outputs/web/.next`; restore reruns Bun install against the same cache, shrinking compressed snapshots from about 150 MB to roughly 1–10 MB and preserving hardlink dedup. Agent instructions now say to use `bun add <pkg>`, never `--no-save`, and verify the dependency lands in `bun.lock`, since snapshots do not carry `node_modules` and `bun.lock` is the source of truth on wake.
- A Craft PR shrinks the sandbox container by dropping the AWS CLI layer, moving snapshot streaming to `s5cmd pipe` / `s5cmd cat`, SHA-pinning the `node:20-slim` base and copied `bun` / `s5cmd` binaries, and pinning opencode installs by version. The snapshot sidecar derives `S3_ENDPOINT_URL` from `AWS_ENDPOINT_URL` so `s5cmd` targets MinIO correctly in dev/CI, and snapshot failures now include clearer `s5cmd` diagnostics. The prod sandbox image is about 717 MB versus 915 MB before, and CI builds set `ENABLE_SKILLS=false` to skip LibreOffice, poppler, fonts, and global `pptxgenjs`, producing a roughly 581 MB image. The recorded kind benchmark shows prod cold p50 around 28.8s and CI cold p50 around 22.8s, while warm spinup stays about 900ms. The default Python venv no longer includes heavier ML/CV packages such as `opencv-python`, `scikit-learn`, `scikit-image`, `scipy`, `xgboost-cpu`, `markitdown`, `seaborn`, and `matplotlib-venn`; agents should `pip install` those only when needed, while the core `numpy` / `pandas` / `matplotlib` / `Pillow` / `pdfplumber` / `openpyxl` / `python-pptx` stack remains. A new `docs/craft/sandbox/image-and-spinup.md` doc and `bench-sandbox-spinup.sh` harness record the image and cold/warm spinup benchmarks.
- A Craft CI PR enables the dormant Kubernetes snapshot coverage in `pr-craft-k8s-tests.yml`: `test_snapshot_restore.py` (8 create/restore snapshot tests) and `test_idle_cleanup.py` (6 idle-cleanup snapshot-flow tests) now run in CI and are included in the workflow `paths:` trigger. `test_snapshot_restore.py` builds its boto3 S3 client from `S3_ENDPOINT_URL` and `S3_AWS_*` so host-side MinIO access does not inherit the in-cluster `AWS_ENDPOINT_URL` and hit DNS resolution errors. The AGENTS.md/opencode.json exclusion assertion is scoped to the session root so legitimate scaffold files such as `outputs/web/AGENTS.md` are not treated as managed root files. Kubernetes snapshot restore now regenerates the `.opencode/skills` and `user_library` symlinks after workspace cleanup, matching the docker backend so later `push_to_sandbox` calls keep skills visible from the session side. The parent `sandbox-bun` branch supplied the missing CI infrastructure by forwarding `AWS_*` env vars to the sandbox sidecar, routing in-cluster MinIO through a manual Kubernetes Service/Endpoints, and pre-creating the snapshot bucket. The re-enabled suite passed end-to-end against the kind cluster in `craft-k8s-tests`.
- Craft has a Docker sandbox backend for docker-compose deployments, and kind/Kubernetes is the canonical Craft dev path. Set `SANDBOX_BACKEND=docker` for docker-compose deployments; `SANDBOX_BACKEND` defaults to `kubernetes`, and `local` now fails at startup with a doc pointer because `LocalSandboxManager` and the local sandbox backend have been removed. Local one-shot tooling is `make craft-up`, `make craft-down`, and `make craft-sandbox-image`; the Kubernetes CI workflow also runs `test_kubernetes_sandbox_file_ops.py`, `test_skill_push.py`, and `test_user_library_sync.py` against a real kind cluster with a 30-minute timeout.
- A Craft PR adds `get_external_app_credentials`, which resolves auth headers for outbound URLs by matching enabled external apps' `upstream_url_patterns` with `re.fullmatch` and rendering the app `auth_template` from org and per-user credentials. It scans enabled apps in id order for deterministic overlapping matches, treats the patterns as match-any, and lets non-string template values pass through. It returns no credentials when no enabled app matches, the app is disabled, required template values are missing, or template rendering fails; invalid upstream URL regex patterns are rejected on update with `OnyxError(INVALID_INPUT)`.
- Craft now has External Apps API endpoints and Craft UI pages behind the craft flag. Admins can create/update, list, and delete org-level apps through `/build/admin/apps`, configure `app_type`, `upstream_url_patterns`, `auth_template`, `organization_credentials`, and `enabled`, and read built-in provider descriptors from `GET /api/build/admin/apps/built-in/options` and `GET /api/build/admin/apps/built-in/options/{app_type}`; `enabled` acts as a kill switch and disabled apps are hidden from users. Users can list exposed enabled apps through `/build/apps`, upsert per-user credentials through `/build/apps/{id}/credentials`, and connect/disconnect built-in OAuth apps from `/craft/v1/apps`, while admins manage apps from `/craft/v1/apps/admin`. The sidebar exposes “My Apps” and admin-gated “Manage Apps” tabs. Org credentials and raw auth templates are not exposed to users; users are authenticated automatically when org credentials cover all required template keys. Built-in Slack, Linear, and Google Calendar external apps use the OAuth provider registry, `GET /api/build/apps/{id}/oauth/start`, `POST /api/build/apps/oauth/callback`, the frontend callback page `/craft/v1/apps/oauth/callback`, and token refresh where the provider supports refresh. They ship as sandbox skill bundles, appear only for authenticated users, update on connect/disconnect, and are injected under reserved `_external_apps/<app_id>-<app_type>/` paths. These external-app bundles render in a separate Connected External Apps section in `AGENTS.md` with token-injection guidance, remain hidden from skills endpoints and the skills tab, and are removed when the backing external app is unavailable or deleted.
- Craft Kubernetes sandboxes route outbound egress through an in-cluster `sandbox-proxy`, which resolves sandbox pod IPs to user/session identity and forwards non-gated traffic unchanged. The backend dependency group includes `mitmproxy==11.0.2` for sandbox-egress proxy work; it is not a top-level project dependency, so the `model_server` container does not install mitmproxy or its transitive additions. It is pinned at 11.0.2 because 11.1+ requires Python 3.12, and `[tool.uv] override-dependencies` keeps the backend on its newer brotli, h11, cryptography, h2, and hyperframe versions. Craft action approvals now gate Slack `chat.postMessage` egress through the proxy. A gated request creates an `ActionApproval`, announces an `approval_requested` event over the per-session live SSE stream, waits up to 3 minutes for an approve/reject decision, then forwards approved requests or returns 403 for rejected/expired ones. The approvals API exposes per-session listing/live endpoints and a decision endpoint; the gate fails open for non-gated egress, unknown sandbox IPs, and idle sessions so unrelated traffic such as package installs continues.
- Craft also has an experimental end-to-end egress interception PoC under `experiments/egress-poc` for policy enforcement and credential injection without exposing secrets to the sandbox. It includes a mitmproxy-based policy proxy, a FastAPI credential broker, CA tooling, Docker Compose and Kubernetes demos, explicit proxy mode via `HTTP[S]_PROXY`, and transparent mode via `iptables` DNAT with reject-by-default behavior.
- The Document Sets docs describe Document Sets as bundles of logically connected documents that can be used as search filters to control the scope of information Onyx searches over. Admins create them from Admin Panel → Document Sets by naming/describing the set and adding one or more Connectors. Listed use cases include grouping related knowledge, assigning whole document collections to Agents so they reference only relevant knowledge, associating sets with User Groups for access control, and letting users search within specific collections. A Discord clarification adds that document sets are logical groupings of connectors and do not duplicate or re-index the underlying documents; a single connector and its documents can be referenced by multiple document sets while the documents are stored once. Document sets are scoped at the connector/`cc_pair_id` level, not at individual document or metadata level, so metadata-based sets such as “all docs where year = 2024” require organizing ingestion/connectors by that grouping, such as one File Connector per year or one connector per desired group. A cross-cutting Agent that should see all documents can use a document set containing all relevant connector IDs. Another Discord clarification says there is no custom metadata tag filtering in the Chat UI on CE or EE; the only Chat UI scoping mechanism is attaching document sets or files to an Agent/Persona, which is document-set/file scoping rather than tag filtering. The tag filter bar for source, time, author, and custom tags exists only in the EE Search UI, not in Chat or Agent creation. Under the hood, attached files are scoped by an internal persona mechanism: indexed chunks can carry a `personas` field, and searches for a persona filter by `persona_id` in Vespa/OpenSearch; this is not user-configurable custom metadata filtering and behaves the same on Vespa and OpenSearch. The same flow can be automated by API: ingest documents with metadata via `POST /api/onyx-api/ingestion`, create document sets via `POST /api/manage/admin/document-set`, and assign them to agents via `PATCH /api/manage/admin/persona`. The Ingestion API is an upsert, so re-sending the same document `id` updates the existing document instead of creating duplicates; repeated automation runs are safe if document IDs are stable.
- The Language Models docs describe an Admin Panel → Language Models page for choosing which LLM providers the workspace can use, which models are visible, and which models are the default or fast option for chat, agents, and other text workflows. Supported provider categories include direct providers such as OpenAI and Anthropic; cloud platforms/aggregators such as Azure OpenAI, Bedrock, Vertex AI, OpenRouter, LiteLLM Proxy, and Bifrost; self-hosted/local runtimes such as Ollama and LM Studio; and OpenAI-compatible custom providers. Image generation and voice are configured separately.
- A Discord question asks whether Onyx can use a different model for image analysis than the default LLM, such as keeping a larger default chat model while using a smaller vision model for image analysis. The supported configuration path still needs clarification.
- A Discord question flags that a user does not see a temperature option in the frontend LLM popover and asks how to enable it. The expected availability and configuration path for temperature controls in the UI still needs clarification.
- A Discord report says a user does not have `/admin/workspace-settings`; the expected availability and route for workspace settings still needs clarification.
- A Discord question says the Indexing Settings page in Onyx `3.3.6` does not show an option referenced from a merge; the version availability of that Indexing Settings option still needs clarification.
- A Discord clarification says OpenAI and Anthropic can appear as default providers using Onyx's own API keys; this is intentional, included in the plan, and subject to Onyx Cloud weekly usage limits. Onyx Cloud weekly LLM usage limits are per-tenant/workspace, not per-seat, so one heavy user can consume the shared weekly allowance and adding paid seats does not increase the cap. Reported limits include stricter Trial caps of about $32/week in LLM cost, 400 API calls/week, 80 non-streaming API calls/week, and 400k chunks indexed/week; Business paid plans have higher caps, including about 40,000 API calls/week and 160 non-streaming API calls/week. Limits reset on a weekly rolling window, and exceeding the limit blocks further LLM requests until the window resets. BYOK is the recommended workaround: adding your own OpenAI or Anthropic API key from Admin Panel → Configuration → LLM bypasses Onyx’s weekly limits, and the customer pays the provider directly for that usage; teams can also contact hello@onyx.app to ask for a manual tenant limit adjustment. A related Discord question asks where users can see these limits in the app and whether usage with Onyx's keys is free; the exact in-app visibility/location for the limit counter still needs clarification.
- The LM Studio docs describe a built-in Onyx integration for models served by LM Studio. Admins configure it from Admin Panel → Configuration → Language Models by selecting LM Studio, setting a Display Name and API Base URL such as `http://localhost:1234`, and Onyx automatically discovers the loaded models, including capabilities such as vision/reasoning and context length. LM Studio runs on port 1234 by default via `lms server start --port 1234`; if LM Studio runs on a different machine than Onyx, the LM Studio server must be reachable from the Onyx host. Admins can choose visible models in Advanced Options and make the provider public or restrict it to admins and explicitly assigned user groups.
- The Bifrost docs describe configuring Bifrost as a language model gateway from Admin Panel → Configuration → Language Models. Onyx connects to the Bifrost gateway through its `/v1/models` endpoint, can use an API Base URL and optional API Key, and imports the model IDs and display names exposed by Bifrost. Admins can choose which imported models are visible to users and can make the provider public or restrict it to admins and explicitly assigned user groups.
- The LiteLLM Proxy docs describe configuring LiteLLM Proxy as a language model gateway from Admin Panel → Configuration → Language Models. Onyx reads available models from the LiteLLM Proxy `/v1/models` endpoint, using the proxy API Base URL and API Key; the local default URL is commonly `http://localhost:4000`. Admins select LiteLLM Proxy, provide a Display Name, API Base URL, and API Key, then click Fetch Available Models to import the model IDs exposed by the proxy. They can choose visible models in Advanced Options and make the provider public or restrict it to admins and explicitly assigned user groups.
- The Image Generation docs describe a dedicated Admin Panel configuration page at Configuration → Image Generation for enabling the Image Generation Action. The feature creates PNG images from user prompts, renders them in chat, and lets users download them. Supported providers/models include OpenAI or Azure OpenAI for GPT Image 1.5, GPT Image 1, and DALL-E 3, plus Vertex/Google for Nano Banana and Nano Banana Pro; GPT Image 1.5 is described as best for production-quality generation with strong prompt control and in-image text/layouts, GPT Image 1 as strong for prompt adherence, Nano Banana as fast and efficient for creative exploration/simple tasks, Nano Banana Pro as high-fidelity 4K output for complex tasks, and DALL-E 3 as older but useful for imaginative/rich styles. The docs say Stability AI support may be added in the future. Once a default image generation model is configured, any AI model in Onyx can invoke the Image Generation Action when a user asks for an image; the docs recommend being explicit when prompting for specific Actions.
- The Code Execution docs describe Code Execution as a built-in Action for Agents to write and run Python for complex calculations, data analysis on uploaded files such as CSVs/spreadsheets, file generation, and visualizations that render in the Chat UI. No configuration is required, but Code Execution must be toggled on in a specific Agent’s configuration. The code execution server is connected by default, can be disconnected or reconnected from the Admin Panel, and exposes health and connection status there. Execution runs in a secure sandbox with pre-installed libraries such as numpy, pandas, scipy, and matplotlib; network access is disabled, filesystem access is restricted, and resource limits/timeouts are applied. The LLM decides when to invoke Code Execution based on the user’s query, so users do not need to explicitly call it.
- A Discord diagnostic for chat hangs says to check whether the model is emitting a tool call named `python`; that specific tool name may not exist in the enabled Onyx tool set, causing the chat to wait on a nonexistent tool response. One observed hang stopped at `[Tool Call] name=python` where the model tried to run a subprocess and `pip install fpdf2`, which is another sign the model may be hallucinating an external Python/code-execution tool or trying to create a PDF through an unavailable path. A later Discord follow-up clarifies that this kind of block is a tool call generated by the LLM inside Onyx: the model is trying to use Python/code execution to install `fpdf2` and create a PDF. For diagnosis, capture the full tool-call output from Onyx, including stdout, stderr, and return code; `Return code: 0` indicates the tool ran successfully, while `Return code: 1` or an exception indicates an execution failure. If the tool call fails silently or never returns a visible result, suspected causes include the tool result not being returned correctly to the model or the model retrying the same tool loop, as previously seen with Gemma4. Suggested mitigations are to disable unused tools in the Assistant/Chat configuration, especially anything resembling code execution or Python if it is not needed, leave only Search enabled for document-retrieval use cases, ask for text/Markdown instead of file/PDF creation when file generation is not required, or try a model/configuration with tools disabled. The note also flags that this can come from an assistant system prompt or from a model hallucinating a familiar external tool.
- The MCP Actions docs describe an Admin Panel MCP Actions tab where admins can add MCP servers, configure authentication, validate connections, list available tools, and choose which tools are available for Agents across the organization. Adding a server requires a server name, description, and MCP Server URL that is reachable from the Onyx instance; most URLs end in `/mcp`, or `/sse` for older servers. Self-hosted MCP servers must run in HTTP transport mode because Onyx does not currently support connecting via stdio. Onyx creates newly added servers in a disconnected state until authentication is configured and the connection is validated.
- The MCP Actions docs list four authentication options for connecting Onyx to MCP servers: No Auth, API Key, OAuth, and Pass-Through OAuth. API Key mode can use a shared key for all users or individual user-provided keys, with admins able to configure arbitrary header patterns for individual-key mode. OAuth can use Dynamic Client Registration when supported, or a manually created OAuth app with Client ID and Client Secret when DCR is unavailable. Pass-Through OAuth is available only when the Onyx instance authenticates via OAuth, and passes the user’s OAuth access token to the MCP server as an `Authorization: Bearer` header.
- PR #11278 fixes per-user OAuth setup for deferred-auth MCP servers, such as GCP Logging at `https://logging.googleapis.com/mcp`, that allow unauthenticated initialization/tool listing but require OAuth before protected tool calls. When no user OAuth tokens exist, connect now proactively discovers OAuth metadata, uses Dynamic Client Registration when needed, starts a PKCE flow, and surfaces the browser authorization URL; the callback exchanges tokens and clears stored flow state. Reconnects preserve existing per-user OAuth tokens and headers unless credentials actually change, admins can pass extra `oauth_authorization_url_params` into the authorization URL, and the previous SDK-driven OAuth path remains as a fallback.
- The MCP Actions docs also note that Onyx can act as an MCP server for connecting Claude, Cursor, and other AI tools to the Onyx knowledge base.
- The Actions overview docs describe an Admin Panel sidebar Actions tab where Actions can be viewed and configured. Built-in Actions are Internal Search, Web Search, Code Execution, and Image Generation; Web Search provider choices listed there include Google, Serper, Exa, and optional Firecrawl. Agents must be configured to have access to an Action before they can automatically decide when to invoke it, and built-in Actions are also available in the general Chat experience.
- A Discord clarification says Onyx lets the LLM decide whether indexed-document search is needed for each query by default, so the model may skip search if it thinks it can answer from training data; this can be more noticeable with smaller or weaker local models. For self-hosted deployments that need consistent retrieval, setting `DISABLE_LLM_CHOOSE_SEARCH=True` and restarting containers forces Onyx to always run search against indexed documents instead of leaving that decision to the model.
- A Discord troubleshooting note says that when search itself is slow, rather than the LLM skipping search, admins can enable timing diagnostics with `LOG_LEVEL=debug`, `LOG_VESPA_TIMING_INFORMATION=true`, and `LOG_ENDPOINT_LATENCY=true`, then restart. The resulting timing breakdown shows where latency is spent, such as query expansion, Vespa/OpenSearch search, LLM document selection, and LLM context expansion. The primary place to watch these SearchTool timing logs is the `api_server` container, for example with `docker logs -f onyx-stack-api_server-1 2>&1 | grep -i "searchtool\|search\|latency\|error"` or by tailing `docker logs -f onyx-stack-api_server-1` at debug level. The `background` container is worth checking for indexing health or OpenSearch connectivity errors with `docker logs onyx-stack-background-1 --tail 200`, and `model_server` can be checked if embedding-model issues are suspected. With small corpuses such as around 40 documents, retrieval should usually be near-instant; likely bottlenecks include local reranking without a GPU, a self-hosted embedding model without a GPU, LLM-based document/chunk selection, and query rephrasing. A related Discord question asks whether dockerized Onyx can offload embedding to the GPU; the supported Docker/GPU configuration path still needs clarification. For model-specific failures, run the same query back-to-back with a failing model and a working model and compare the timing logs; high `LLM doc selection` points to model-dependent document selection, high `Query expansion` points to query rephrasing, and low chunks returned across all models points to a retrieval/recall issue. Suggested quick wins include disabling LLM chunk filtering with `DISABLE_LLM_CHUNK_FILTER=True`, disabling LLM query rephrasing with `DISABLE_LLM_QUERY_REPHRASE=True`, disabling reranking when it is not useful for the corpus size, or switching embeddings to a cloud provider such as Cohere or OpenAI.
- A Discord troubleshooting note for tool-call errors says to inspect Docker logs in real time while reproducing the request. Use `docker ps` to list active containers if names are unclear, then `docker logs <container> --tail 100 -f` or `docker logs onyx-stack-api_server-1 --tail 200 -f` to follow recent logs. For Onyx, the most relevant containers are `onyx-stack-api_server-1` for backend, LLM, and tool-call errors; `onyx-stack-background-1` for background tasks; and `onyx-stack-inference_model_server-1` for inference-model issues.
- The Web Search docs add that Web Search is already active on Onyx Cloud with no additional configuration required. For self-hosted deployments, admins configure it from Admin Panel → Web Search, connect a search provider such as Exa AI, Serper, or Google PSE, optionally configure a web crawler such as the built-in Onyx web crawler or Firecrawl, set default providers when multiple providers are configured, and ensure the Agent has the Web Search Action enabled.
- A Slack question asks what the differences are between the scrape methods in the Web Connector; the supported method distinctions and recommended selection criteria still need clarification.
- The Actions & MCP docs describe Actions as a way to extend Onyx Agents with external-system capabilities. Onyx includes built-in Actions for Internal Search, Web Search,

## Summary

  - 🔴 Should commit — critical
  - 🟡 Should commit — moderate
  - 🟢 Should commit — nit
  - ✓ Should no-change — already covered
  - ↩ Should no-change — extra info, not worth inclusion
  - ⊘ Should be irrelevant — wrong selection

# Scania SharePoint Connector Issues — Living Document

_Last updated: 2026-05-21_

This is a living document describing the issues Scania has run into with the SharePoint connector. All Onyx-indexed communication about Scania in the `#customer-support` Slack channel that involves SharePoint is cited here.

> **Citation note:** The references below are Slack / meeting links surfaced from Onyx search. In several cases Onyx exposed the indexed Slack result link and thread context, but not all original attachments/screenshots or complete thread metadata.

---

# Overview and useful context

As of the latest retrieved `#customer-support` evidence, Scania was on **Onyx `v3.3.0`**, had **one active SharePoint connector**, and was still experiencing **indexing throughput / connector reliability issues**. Justin noted that this active connector “keeps hitting issues,” that Scania likely runs on Kubernetes, and that Onyx needed to provide an upgrade strategy. A suspected deployment anomaly was also noted: the **OpenSearch migration page was missing**, raising concern that Scania might be on `v3.3.0` without an OpenSearch container. Evan was assigned to continue looking through logs and SharePoint issue details. [[5]](https://onyx-company.slack.com/archives/C09B4PBPFN2/p1778686355854159?thread_ts=1778686355.854159)

The prior May 11 update showed meaningful progress: Scania devtest had been upgraded to `v3.3.0`; Vespa memory had been increased from `32Gi` to `48Gi`; old Vespa `507 Insufficient Storage` / feed-blocking had stopped being the active blocker; docfetching workers were stable after a probe-timeout change; and a local SharePoint hotfix changed unauthorized `.aspx` page handling from “abort the whole connector run” to “record as per-document failure.” However, the connector named **`SharePoint all ASPX sites since first of March`** was still failing on Microsoft Graph `404 itemNotFound` for `/teams/Almedalentrip`, interpreted as a missing or invalid SharePoint site in the crawl scope. [[2]](https://onyx-company.slack.com/archives/C09B4PBPFN2/p1778522482318179?thread_ts=1778522442.236789)

Subsequent SharePoint connector work in PR #11266 adds another relevant failure-handling improvement: Graph `HTTP 423 notAllowed` for admin-locked or M365-archived sites is now treated as a per-site failure, so tenant indexing continues to the next site. This is not evidence that Scania hit a 423, but it is relevant to Scania's broad tenant crawl risk because `getAllSites` can surface sites the app cannot read.

Separate docfetching observability work in PR #11294, cherry-picked to `release/v4.0` by PR #11296, fixes `document_count` so it increments for each queued batch. Builds with this fix should have docfetching logs and metrics that reflect the real number of documents processed.

There is an apparent but explainable tension between the May 11 and May 13 updates: on May 11, Lindsey relayed that Jim said they seemed to be “up and running” at **180–200 docs/minute**, while the same May 11 update still listed the `Almedalentrip` Graph `404` as the active run-level blocker for a specific connector. [[2]](https://onyx-company.slack.com/archives/C09B4PBPFN2/p1778522482318179?thread_ts=1778522442.236789) By May 13, Justin again said Scania still had throughput issues and only one active SharePoint connector that kept hitting issues. [[5]](https://onyx-company.slack.com/archives/C09B4PBPFN2/p1778686355854159?thread_ts=1778686355.854159) This likely means Scania saw partial throughput improvement but had not reached a stable, fully resolved state.

## Apr. 28 engineering performance analysis

In `eng-infra`, Scania reported about **14 docs/minute** on `v3.2.1`, despite multiple docfetching replicas. Only one docfetching pod was materially busy, and logs showed repeated SharePoint permission/external-access work such as “Getting external access for ...” and `permission_utils.py ... Processing group ...`. [[13]](https://onyx-company.slack.com/archives/C097NBWMY8Y/p1777395633493289?thread_ts=1777395633.493289)

Engineering explained that SharePoint data retrieval is serialized per connector: `connector_doc_fetching_task` is expected to run as one long-lived task on a single worker. Recommended workaround: split SharePoint into multiple connectors by site/drive/scope. [[13]](https://onyx-company.slack.com/archives/C097NBWMY8Y/p1777395633493289?thread_ts=1777395633.493289)

# Recurring patterns and likely root causes

## 1. Permission-aware SharePoint indexing is the central systemic issue

Scania requires permission-preserving SharePoint indexing across a very large and messy SharePoint estate. This forces Onyx to fetch SharePoint permissions, role assignments, external access, and group membership information. These operations repeatedly appear in stack traces and performance logs. [[1]](https://onyx-company.slack.com/archives/C09B4PBPFN2/p1776696156151729?thread_ts=1776696156.151729), [[3]](https://onyx-company.slack.com/archives/C09B4PBPFN2/p1777566141560249?thread_ts=1777564268.604939), [[13]](https://onyx-company.slack.com/archives/C097NBWMY8Y/p1777395633493289?thread_ts=1777395633.493289), [[14]](https://app.fireflies.ai/view/01KQATHEAM3DR2AHS5VKRGAMHF?t=2048.29)

Evidence includes `AIatScania` and `SJPIndependentDealers` `401`s while fetching role assignments, R&D hub group/member traversal failures, logs dominated by permission work, and faster organization-public connector performance because it skipped permission fetching.

## 2. Unauthorized `.aspx` pages used to abort connector runs

A single unauthorized `.aspx` page could fail the entire connector run. This showed up in `AIatScania` and `SJPIndependentDealers` incidents. The May 11 hotfix changed behavior so page-level permission failures become per-document failures instead of run-level aborts. [[1]](https://onyx-company.slack.com/archives/C09B4PBPFN2/p1776696156151729?thread_ts=1776696156.151729), [[3]](https://onyx-company.slack.com/archives/C09B4PBPFN2/p1777566141560249?thread_ts=1777564268.604939), [[2]](https://onyx-company.slack.com/archives/C09B4PBPFN2/p1778522482318179?thread_ts=1778522442.236789)

## 3. Invalid, missing, locked, or inaccessible sites in broad crawl scope can cause Graph site-level failures

Broad crawl scope included paths Graph could not resolve, e.g. `/teams/Plymothepsvnner` and `/teams/Almedalentrip`. These appear to be deleted, renamed, inaccessible, misspelled, or otherwise invalid sites. [[1]](https://onyx-company.slack.com/archives/C09B4PBPFN2/p1776696156151729?thread_ts=1776696156.151729), [[2]](https://onyx-company.slack.com/archives/C09B4PBPFN2/p1778522482318179?thread_ts=1778522442.236789)

A later SharePoint connector fix, PR #11266, specifically handles Graph `HTTP 423 notAllowed` for admin-locked or M365-archived sites as per-site failures instead of tenant-run aborts. The same PR notes that `getAllSites` can surface sites the app cannot read; in builds with this fix, those 423 sites should be recorded and skipped rather than blocking the rest of the tenant crawl.

## 4. Throughput bottleneck is mostly SharePoint fetch/permissions, not general compute

Earlier suspicion included CPU embeddings and AWS sizing, but later evidence points strongly to SharePoint retrieval and permission sync. On Apr. 28, only one docfetching pod was busy despite multiple replicas, and engineering explained that one connector’s SharePoint fetch stage runs as a single long-lived task. [[13]](https://onyx-company.slack.com/archives/C097NBWMY8Y/p1777395633493289?thread_ts=1777395633.493289)

## 5. SharePoint API rate limiting is suspected but not proven

There is circumstantial evidence that SharePoint API latency/rate-limit pressure matters, especially given permission-heavy REST/Graph calls, but retrieved records do not show explicit `429 Too Many Requests` errors. Treat as a high-priority hypothesis requiring metrics, not as a proven root cause. [[13]](https://onyx-company.slack.com/archives/C097NBWMY8Y/p1777395633493289?thread_ts=1777395633.493289), [[14]](https://app.fireflies.ai/view/01KQATHEAM3DR2AHS5VKRGAMHF?t=2048.29)

## 6. Deployment/version gaps delayed fixes

Scania moved from `v2.12.6` to `v3.2.1` to `v3.3.0`, while fixes and diagnostics were being identified. Old versions lacked embedding swap, permission sync was not running in `v3.2.1`, local hotfixes were applied in `v3.3.0`, and missing OpenSearch/migration state may block moving to versions with better metrics. [[1]](https://onyx-company.slack.com/archives/C09B4PBPFN2/p1776696156151729?thread_ts=1776696156.151729), [[3]](https://onyx-company.slack.com/archives/C09B4PBPFN2/p1777566141560249?thread_ts=1777564268.604939), [[2]](https://onyx-company.slack.com/archives/C09B4PBPFN2/p1778522482318179?thread_ts=1778522442.236789), [[5]](https://onyx-company.slack.com/archives/C09B4PBPFN2/p1778686355854159?thread_ts=1778686355.854159)

## 7. Scania’s security model and data scale make this a difficult customer environment

Scania’s security model rejects broad `read all`, asks for `site select`, and raises concerns about OneDrive, DLP, sensitivity labels, encrypted files, permission-change lag, and data egress. Scania’s SharePoint estate may be extremely large and decentralized, with related meeting context discussing up to 150 million documents. [[6]](https://onyx-company.slack.com/archives/C09B4PBPFN2/p1772552968781719), [[7]](https://onyx-company.slack.com/archives/C09B4PBPFN2/p1773250716080289), [[14]](https://app.fireflies.ai/view/01KQATHEAM3DR2AHS5VKRGAMHF?t=2048.29)

# Architecture

## Containers

| Container | Role |
|---|---|
| `postgres` | Postgres 17. Stores users, sessions, ACL, trigger config, events, ingest settings. Schema managed by Alembic — `init_db()` runs `alembic upgrade head` on every boot. |
| `redis` | Redis 7. Backs the three Redis Streams task queues (`documents`, `triggers`, `lightweight_maintenance`). |
| `opensearch` | OpenSearch 2.x. BM25 full-text search index (`wiki-docs`). One document per `.md` file; fields: `path` (keyword), `title` (text, boost 3×), `body` (text). |
| `backend` | FastAPI app on :8080 (uvicorn, 2 workers). Hosts the REST API and MCP server. |
| `worker-documents` | Same image as backend. Runs `app.tasks.run_worker documents` — LLM-bound doc-update tasks. |
| `worker-triggers` | Same image as backend. Runs `app.tasks.run_worker triggers` — trigger evaluation and fan-out. |
| `worker-lightweight-maintenance` | Same image as backend. Runs `app.tasks.run_worker lightweight_maintenance` — BM25 reindex, agent-activity cleanup, hourly reconcile sweep. |
| `frontend` | Next.js + TypeScript UI on :3000. |
| `nginx` | Reverse proxy on :80 — `/api/*` → backend, everything else → frontend. |

## Volumes

| Volume | Mount | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `wiki-data` | `/data/wiki` | Git-backed wiki working tree. Backend shells out to `git`. Backend + all workers share an RWO mount and must co-schedule. |

## Storage

- **Wiki content** — files in `wiki-data`, committed to git on every write via `app.wiki.git`. Every write is a real git commit; history is always consistent with the working tree.
- **App state** — Postgres: users, MCP sessions/tokens, ACL entries, trigger definitions, trigger events, ingest settings, agent-activity log. Schema in `backend/app/db/models.py`; migrations in `backend/app/db/migrations/versions/`.
- **Search index** — OpenSearch `wiki-docs` index. Populated by `app.tasks.reindex.index_path` after every doc commit and by an hourly reconcile sweep (`reconcile_bm25_index`). Visibility filtering applied post-query in Python via `acl.filter_paths_in_python`.
- **Task queues** — Redis Streams. Three queues: `documents` (LLM-bound, slow), `triggers` (fast fan-out), `lightweight_maintenance` (sub-second upkeep). Each queue has its own dedicated worker container.

## Evaluation harness

Offline evals for wiki-reading and wiki-writing agents live under `backend/evals/`, outside `tests/` because live runs hit real LLMs and are parameterized by `(provider, model)`. The harness covers `wiki_updater.process_instruction`, `wiki_updater.reconcile_document`, `ingest_selector.select_candidates`, and the external agent path that drives `update_doc_nl`.

The evals split each surface into **WHEN** decisions, such as `NO_CHANGE`, change, or `IRRELEVANT`, and **HOW** quality, such as preserving facts and avoiding bloat. Deterministic scorers include `trigger_class_match`, `bloat_ratio`, `markdown_valid`, and `selector_set_metrics`; LLM-judge scorers use `app.llm.client.complete` for `facts_present` and `facts_preserved`.

The shared runner in `evals/_cli.py` fans `(case × model × run)` trials across a `ThreadPoolExecutor` with a copied `contextvars.Context` per worker, so `use_model` overrides are thread-local and agent code does not change between models. Dry-run stubs patch module-global `client.complete` / `.stream` once around the pool, and JSONL output is sorted by `(case_id, provider, model, run_index)` for stable runs. `evals-smoke.yml` runs `--dry-run` on PRs without API keys, while `evals-nightly.yml` runs the live matrix with `EVAL_*_API_KEY` secrets and pushes results through `app.tracing.braintrust.push_experiment`.

Real-traffic ingest samples can be labeled with `backend/scripts/eval_labeler.html`. The browser labeler writes labels, coverage notes, and source/wiki/diff summaries back into the original `.jsonl` rows via the File System Access API; summaries are generated manually per sample with a memory-only Anthropic key and are deduplicated across rows with identical source or wiki content.

## Data flow: Onyx pushes a document

```
ONYX                                       AGENT WIKI
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

                                           Admin UI
                                             └─ POST /admin/ingest/regenerate-key
                                                     │
                                                ingest_settings (Postgres)
                                                api_key = secrets.token_urlsafe(32)
                                                     │
                                                     │ admin copies base URL + key
                                                     ▼
env vars:
AGENT_WIKI_ENABLED=true      ◀────────────  AGENT_WIKI_BASE_URL
AGENT_WIKI_BASE_URL                          AGENT_WIKI_API_KEY
AGENT_WIKI_API_KEY

┌─────────────────────────┐
│  Onyx indexer           │
│  (Celery task, fires    │  POST /api/documents/ingest
│   after each indexing   │  Authorization: Bearer <api_key>
│   batch)                │─────────────────────────────────▶  FastAPI backend
│                         │  {content, title, source_type,        │
│  skips if:              │   metadata, updated_at}               │ validate bearer token
│  - multi-tenant         │                                       │ check max_doc_chars
│  - non-public connector │◀─────────────────────────────────────  202 Accepted
│  - doc too large        │                                       │
└─────────────────────────┘                                       │ enqueue
                                                                  ▼
                                                       documents_queue (Redis Streams)
                                                                  │
                                                                  ▼
                                                       worker-documents
                                                       process_pushed_document()
                                                                  │
                                                       resolve page + LLM update
                                                                  │
                                                           git commit
                                                                  │
                                                     ┌────────────┴────────────┐
                                                     ▼                         ▼
                                          lightweight_maintenance_queue    triggers_queue
                                          index_path()                fan_out_trigger_eval()
                                                  │
                                                  ▼
                                             OpenSearch
```

The ingest reconciliation step uses a typed `submit_results` tool call for per-candidate actions rather than parsing free-text result blocks. Edit application still uses targeted FIND/REPLACE blocks, with a trailing-whitespace-normalized fallback so minor spacing differences do not cause an otherwise valid edit to miss.

## Data flow: user edits a doc

1. UI saves via `PUT /api/documents/<path>` or agent tool calls `commit_file`.
2. Backend commits to git via `app.wiki.git.commit_file`.
3. `notify.after_doc_write` fires: enqueues `index_path` on `lightweight_maintenance_queue` + `fan_out_trigger_eval` on `triggers_queue` + publishes MCP pub-sub event.
4. `worker-lightweight-maintenance` picks up `index_path`, reads body from git, upserts into OpenSearch.
5. `worker-triggers` picks up `fan_out_trigger_eval`, evaluates delta triggers scoped to the doc and parent dirs, records `trigger.fire` events.

## Data flow: scheduled trigger

1. In-process periodic scheduler on `worker-triggers` fires `evaluate_scheduled_triggers` at minute 0 (hourly). Running more than one replica per queue would double-fire it.
2. Handler loads enabled `kind=schedule` triggers due now, runs the configured action, records `trigger.fire`.

## Open questions

- **Cost** — every Onyx connector update will trigger an LLM pass on the relevant wiki page. Need batching / debounce to avoid runaway cost at high connector volume.
- **Doc bloat / loss** — the document-updater agent must not grow docs unboundedly or drop important context. System prompt enforces this, and the new offline eval harness now includes bloat-bait and loss-bait cases with `bloat_ratio`, `facts_present`, and `facts_preserved` scorers. The current v0 datasets include 30 `wiki_updater` cases, 5 `ingest_selector` cases, and 24 external-agent scenarios, and should grow to roughly 200 cases once the `INGEST_EVAL_LOGGING` sample flow is available.
- **`process_pushed_document` routing** — how the agent picks which wiki page(s) to update from a raw Onyx document push is not yet implemented. LLM-routed via the document-updater agent.

- What are the volumes for the top source types

## Some random notes
- Logic to determine what to pass over should live on the Onyx side
- It will be a better update on average if we can pass diffs along with the docs. Ideally a section above/below the area with the diff and handling merges where multiple parts are edited.
  - Something like up to 2000 subword tokens above and below the diff might be good

## Current implementation
- BM25 candidates with a cutoff
  - This is probably reasonable however BM25 was built for queries, not documents. Something should maybe be done here.
- Per candidate page:
  - There are classifications like NO_CHANGE, IRRELEVANT, or applying a new body. The batch reconciler now collects these decisions through a typed `submit_results` tool call instead of parsing fragile free-text result blocks.
  - Edit application still uses targeted FIND/REPLACE blocks, with a trailing-whitespace-normalized fallback so minor spacing differences do not cause an otherwise valid edit to miss.
- Offline evals now live under `backend/evals/` and explicitly test both **WHEN** to update and **HOW** good the update is.
  - Current scorers relevant to bloat and drift include `bloat_ratio`, `markdown_valid`, `facts_present`, and `facts_preserved`.
  - The v0 `wiki_updater` dataset includes 30 cases across NO_CHANGE / CHANGE / IRRELEVANT, including bloat-bait and loss-bait examples.

- Agent loop shoud only have tool calls to do single or multi-edit, it should have looping behavior until it outputs finish or hits a max
- I would look pretty heavily into prompt tuning, likely this can prevent the bloat pretty strongly.
  - Some other things to include in the prompt:

    - Instructions to not scope-creep the document

- We can have a separate loop to prune the doc back to the length and set topics.
- Can freeze the doc after like some small number of commits (max 10), max time delay from creation (1 week).

### Tools
- edit
- multi_edit
- mark_irrelevant
- finish

- If a doc gets too many updates, it should get flagged to the owner.

# Deployments of Agent Wiki
This doc provides an overview of how to deploy Agent Wiki locally and on cloud.

## Helm chart

The Agent Wiki Helm chart version is `0.3.18`. This chart package includes the `INGEST_EVAL_LOGGING` environment variable in the worker pod templates; dev-wiki sets it to `true` so ingest reconciler examples are logged.

## macOS Run-Agent launcher release

Agent Wiki ships a signed, notarized, and stapled macOS launcher app, `AgentWikiLauncher.app`, for the Run-Agent flow. The build script `scripts/build-app.sh` creates a universal binary, builds the app bundle with `osacompile`, signs the inner Mach-O, applet, and bundle, submits it with `notarytool submit --wait`, staples it, and writes `dist/AgentWikiLauncher.zip`. `scripts/build-app.sh` is the only supported signing path; `scripts/release-mac.sh` has been removed and should not be referenced by release docs or commands.

The reusable workflow `.github/workflows/release-agentwiki-launcher-go.yml` handles launcher signing and notarization. It assumes the AWS signing role via OIDC and reads the Apple signing secrets from AWS Secrets Manager under `deploy/apple-*`. It can be run manually with `workflow_dispatch` or called by other workflows with `workflow_call`.

The launcher workflow uses `actions/cache@v4` as a content-addressed cache for `dist/`, keyed by `hashFiles('packages/agentwiki-launcher-go/**')`. When the launcher source is unchanged, setup-go, AWS OIDC, Apple secret retrieval, and `scripts/build-app.sh` are skipped; the cached notarized artifact is uploaded for downstream backend image builds. A cold launcher build still takes about 5 minutes, while a warm cache hit is about 30 seconds. Stapled `.app` notarization tickets do not expire, and the GitHub Actions cache can evict entries after 7 days.

`docker-build-push.yml` and `nightly-build.yml` call the launcher release workflow, download the notarized artifact, and place it under `backend/static/installers/`. The backend image includes this directory via `backend/Dockerfile`'s `COPY static ./static`, and production serves the zip from `GET /api/installer/app`.

## Launcher deployment go-live checklist

Before cutting a release that includes the macOS launcher:

1. Merge `onyx-dot-app/cloud-deployment-yamls#349` and run `terraform apply` so the least-privilege `agent-wiki-signing` role exists.
2. Set the `AWS_OIDC_ROLE_ARN` repo secret on `onyx-dot-app/agent-wiki` to the Terraform `signing_role_arn` output.
3. Merge the Agent Wiki launcher PR.
4. Cut a `v*` tag so `docker-build-push.yml` runs and bakes `AgentWikiLauncher.zip` into the backend image.
5. Users can then visit `/agents`, download the installer, drag the app to Applications, accept the first-run Pin dialog, and use Run Agent.

`LAUNCHERS_ENABLED=true` is already set in `cloud-deployment-yamls/global-terraform/agent-wiki-infra/app/dev-wiki-values.yaml`; no extra dev-wiki toggle is required.

Adds `backend/evals/` — offline eval suite for the agents that read or write the wiki. Outside `tests/` because runs hit real LLMs and are parameterized by `(provider, model)`.

Surfaces under test:
- `nl_updater.process_instruction` (MCP: NO_CHANGE vs new body)
- `ingest_batch_reconciler.batch_reconcile` (ingest: + IRRELEVANT)
- `ingest_selector.select_candidates` (precision/recall over labeled set)
- External agent driving `update_doc_nl` (WHEN routing + reused HOW scorers)

Two axes per surface: **WHEN** (trigger decision) and **HOW** (output quality).

Scorers:
- Deterministic: `trigger_class_match`, `bloat_ratio`, `markdown_valid`, `selector_set_metrics`, `entity_density_delta`, `diff_addition_ratio`
- LLM-judge via `app.llm.client.complete`: `facts_present`, `facts_preserved` (two-judge panel, majority + tie→False)

Architecture: `evals/_cli.py` is the shared runner skeleton; each surface plugs in `load_cases` + `_run_one` + a dry-run stub. `_cli.run_concurrent` fans every `(case × model × run)` trial out across a `ThreadPoolExecutor` with a copied `contextvars.Context` per worker — `use_model` overrides are thread-local. Dry-run stubs patch the module-global `client.complete`/`.stream` once around the pool to avoid per-worker race. Output JSONL is sorted on `(case_id, provider, model, run_index)` for byte-stable runs.

v0 datasets: 30 wiki_updater cases (NO_CHANGE / CHANGE / IRRELEVANT, bloat-bait, loss-bait), 5 ingest_selector cases, 24 external_agent scenarios. Grows to ~200 once Bo's `INGEST_EVAL_LOGGING` lands.

CI: `evals-smoke.yml` (dry-run + 37 unit tests on PR touching eval code) + `evals-nightly.yml` (live matrix, pushes to Braintrust). Each runner writes its scorer table to `$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY` with the BT experiment URL inline.

Seams honored: LLM through `app.llm.client`; Braintrust SDK only via `app.tracing.braintrust.push_experiment`; `git_sha_for` reads `.git` metadata directly (no subprocess outside `app/wiki/git.py`); pydantic, `%s` formatting, no `typing.Any`. Strict basedpyright + ruff clean.

## How Has This Been Tested?

Static + unit:
- `uv run ruff format --check evals/` — 27 files already formatted
- `uv run --extra dev basedpyright` (whole backend) — 0 errors, 0 warnings
- `pre-commit run --from-ref origin/main --to-ref HEAD` — every hook Passed
- `pytest evals/tests` — 37/37 passing (scorers + reporting unit coverage)

Dry-run smoke on all 3 runners (no API keys, deterministic stub LLM):
- wiki_updater 30/30 cases × 2 surfaces
- ingest_selector 5/5 cases
- external_agent 24/24 scenarios
- `evals.ci_assert_baseline runs/` passes on every output file

Live full matrix run (2026-05-22, concurrency=8, 3 runs/case, post-refactor):

| Surface | Cases × Models × Runs | Wall time | Experiment |
| -- | -- | -- | -- |
| `ingest_selector` | 5 × 2 × 3 = 30 | ~11s | [selector-full-20260522-postrefactor](https://www.braintrust.dev/app/Onyx%202/p/agent-wiki-evals/experiments/selector-full-20260522-postrefactor) |
| `wiki_updater` / `process_instruction` | 17 × 2 × 3 = 102 | ~7 min (shared) | [wiki-updater-full-20260522-postrefactor-process-instruction](https://www.braintrust.dev/app/Onyx%202/p/agent-wiki-evals/experiments/wiki-updater-full-20260522-postrefactor-process-instruction) |
| `wiki_updater` / `reconcile_document` | 13 × 2 × 3 = 78 | ~7 min (shared) | [wiki-updater-full-20260522-postrefactor-reconcile-document](https://www.braintrust.dev/app/Onyx%202/p/agent-wiki-evals/experiments/wiki-updater-full-20260522-postrefactor-reconcile-document) |
| `external_agent` | 24 × 2 × 3 = 144 | ~27 min | [external-agent-full-20260522-postrefactor](https://www.braintrust.dev/app/Onyx%202/p/agent-wiki-evals/experiments/external-agent-full-20260522-postrefactor) |

Headline numbers (mean across 3 runs, scorer ∈ [0, 1] higher = better):

**ingest_selector** (selector pre-filter)
| model | f1 | precision | recall |
| -- | -- | -- | -- |
| `claude-haiku-4-5` | 0.58 | 0.51 | 0.98 |
| `gpt-5-mini` | **0.92** | 0.88 | 1.00 |

→ Haiku over-keeps (precision 0.51, recall ~1.0). Candidate prod swap on a follow-up PR.

**wiki_updater.process_instruction** (MCP write path, 17 cases)
| model | trigger.macro_f1 | facts_present | facts_preserved | bloat |
| -- | -- | -- | -- | -- |
| `claude-sonnet-4-6` | **1.00** | 0.94 | 0.97 | 0.99 |
| `gpt-5` | 0.86 | 0.92 | 0.95 | 1.00 |

→ Sonnet perfect on trigger. GPT-5's trigger.recall[NO_CHANGE] = 0.67 (over-triggers updates that shouldn't fire).

**wiki_updater.reconcile_document** (ingest write path, 13 cases)
| model | trigger.macro_f1 | facts_present | facts_preserved | bloat |
| -- | -- | -- | -- | -- |
| `claude-sonnet-4-6` | 0.90 | 0.80 | **1.00** | 0.99 |
| `gpt-5` | **0.91** | **0.89** | **1.00** | 0.95 |

→ Basically tied. Both perfect on `facts_preserved` (no info loss). Sonnet weaker on `facts_present` (drops some new facts that should land).

**external_agent** (24 scenarios, agent driving `update_doc_nl`)
| model | update_f1 | no_touch | facts_present | facts_preserved | error_rate |
| -- | -- | -- | -- | -- | -- |
| `claude-sonnet-4-6` | **1.00** | 1.00 | **0.93** | 0.86 | **0.00** |
| `gpt-5` | 0.99 | 1.00 | 0.90 | 0.87 | 0.04 |

→ Sonnet perfect routing + zero errors. GPT-5 has 4% crashes (1 in 25 trials). Both lose ~14% of facts that should have been preserved across the agent loop — investigate in follow-up.

# Reindexing

## Problem Statement
- Currently customers that want to turn on advanced features like contextual retrieval or updating to a new embedding model do not have a good time.
- Switching an index currently means running a bunch of connectors in the background and if they fail or credentials have expired, we just cannot recover those docs.
- A better solution would be to port documents directly from the existing (primary) index into the new one

## Requirements
- Pull docs from primary index to a secondary unused index until the secondary is fully populated.
- Instant switchover to avoid downtime
- If we need to include additional information in the primary index for this, we need to make sure we're able to still port from existing indices (or at least have a warning)
  - Can discuss the missing items and workarounds

## Complications
- Some existing representations in the index are not intended for this, some things may need modifications
- There's the issue of the primary index still receiving updates from connectors as we do this so we need to ensure the switchover can happen
- Probably the way to handle it is to mark documents with a "ported" flag or something
- But also if the reindexing fails or something, we maybe don't want to touch every ported doc again to unmark the flag

There's probably a reasonably in depth design session to have for this first

## Summary

Fixes #9746 — OpenSearch rejects index names with uppercase characters. When a custom embedding model has uppercase in its name (e.g. `BAAI/bge-m3`), the derived index name `danswer_chunk_BAAI_bge_m3` fails OpenSearch validation.

## Root Cause

`clean_model_name()` in `search_nlp_models.py` replaces `/`, `-`, `.` but does not lowercase the result:

```python
# Before
return model_str.replace("/", "_").replace("-", "_").replace(".", "_")
# BAAI/bge-m3 -> BAAI_bge_m3  (FAILS - OpenSearch forbids uppercase)

# After
return model_str.replace("/", "_").replace("-", "_").replace(".", "_").lower()
# BAAI/bge-m3 -> baai_bge_m3  (OK)
```

## Testing

- Existing lowercase models: unchanged behavior
- `BAAI/bge-m3`: now produces `baai_bge_m3` instead of `BAAI_bge_m3`
- OpenSearch index creation now succeeds with uppercase model names

Closes #9746

# Overview and useful context

As of the latest retrieved `#customer-support` evidence, Scania was on **Onyx `v3.3.0`**, had **one active SharePoint connector**, and was still experiencing **indexing throughput / connector reliability issues**. Justin noted that this active connector “keeps hitting issues,” that Scania likely runs on Kubernetes, and that Onyx needed to provide an upgrade strategy. A suspected deployment anomaly was also noted: the **OpenSearch migration page was missing**, raising concern that Scania might be on `v3.3.0` without an OpenSearch container. Evan was assigned to continue looking through logs and SharePoint issue details. [[5]](https://onyx-company.slack.com/archives/C09B4PBPFN2/p1778686355854159?thread_ts=1778686355.854159)

The prior May 11 update showed meaningful progress: Scania devtest had been upgraded to `v3.3.0`; Vespa memory had been increased from `32Gi` to `48Gi`; old Vespa `507 Insufficient Storage` / feed-blocking had stopped being the active blocker; docfetching workers were stable after a probe-timeout change; and a local SharePoint hotfix changed unauthorized `.aspx` page handling from “abort the whole connector run” to “record as per-document failure.” However, the connector named **`SharePoint all ASPX sites since first of March`** was still failing on Microsoft Graph `404 itemNotFound` for `/teams/Almedalentrip`, interpreted as a missing or invalid SharePoint site in the crawl scope. [[2]](https://onyx-company.slack.com/archives/C09B4PBPFN2/p1778522482318179?thread_ts=1778522442.236789)

Subsequent SharePoint connector work in PR #11266 adds another relevant failure-handling improvement: Graph `HTTP 423 notAllowed` for admin-locked or M365-archived sites is now treated as a per-site failure, so tenant indexing continues to the next site. This is not evidence that Scania hit a 423, but it is relevant to Scania's broad tenant crawl risk because `getAllSites` can surface sites the app cannot read.

Separate docfetching observability work in PR #11294, cherry-picked to `release/v4.0` by PR #11296, fixes `document_count` so it increments for each queued batch. Builds with this fix should have docfetching logs and metrics that reflect the real number of documents processed.

Persistent indexing work in PR #11301 adds `PERSISTENT_INDEXING=true`, which disables normal failure-volume abort thresholds and keeps per-batch docprocessing recovery for application-level failures. It does not swallow unhandled connector-generator exceptions during docfetching; those still fail the index attempt. Infra, heartbeat, and usage-limit failures also still fail the attempt. Deployment and enabling for Scania should be confirmed before relying on it as a mitigation. [[17]](https://github.com/onyx-dot-app/onyx/pull/11301), [[18]](https://github.com/onyx-dot-app/onyx/pull/11311)

# Recurring patterns and likely root causes

## 1. Permission-aware SharePoint indexing is the central systemic issue

Scania requires permission-preserving SharePoint indexing across a very large and messy SharePoint estate. This forces Onyx to fetch SharePoint permissions, role assignments, external access, and group membership information. These operations repeatedly appear in stack traces and performance logs. [[1]](https://onyx-company.slack.com/archives/C09B4PBPFN2/p1776696156151729?thread_ts=1776696156.151729), [[3]](https://onyx-company.slack.com/archives/C09B4PBPFN2/p1777566141560249?thread_ts=1777564268.604939), [[13]](https://onyx-company.slack.com/archives/C097NBWMY8Y/p1777395633493289?thread_ts=1777395633.493289), [[14]](https://app.fireflies.ai/view/01KQATHEAM3DR2AHS5VKRGAMHF?t=2048.29)

Evidence includes `AIatScania` and `SJPIndependentDealers` `401`s while fetching role assignments, R&D hub group/member traversal failures, logs dominated by permission work, and faster organization-public connector performance because it skipped permission fetching.

## 2. Unauthorized `.aspx` pages used to abort connector runs

A single unauthorized `.aspx` page could fail the entire connector run. This showed up in `AIatScania` and `SJPIndependentDealers` incidents. The May 11 hotfix changed behavior so page-level permission failures become per-document failures instead of run-level aborts. [[1]](https://onyx-company.slack.com/archives/C09B4PBPFN2/p1776696156151729?thread_ts=1776696156.151729), [[3]](https://onyx-company.slack.com/archives/C09B4PBPFN2/p1777566141560249?thread_ts=1777564268.604939), [[2]](https://onyx-company.slack.com/archives/C09B4PBPFN2/p1778522482318179?thread_ts=1778522442.236789)

## 3. Invalid, missing, locked, or inaccessible sites in broad crawl scope can cause Graph site-level failures

Broad crawl scope included paths Graph could not resolve, e.g. `/teams/Plymothepsvnner` and `/teams/Almedalentrip`. These appear to be deleted, renamed, inaccessible, misspelled, or otherwise invalid sites. [[1]](https://onyx-company.slack.com/archives/C09B4PBPFN2/p1776696156151729?thread_ts=1776696156.151729), [[2]](https://onyx-company.slack.com/archives/C09B4PBPFN2/p1778522482318179?thread_ts=1778522442.236789)

A later SharePoint connector fix, PR #11266, specifically handles Graph `HTTP 423 notAllowed` for admin-locked or M365-archived sites as per-site failures instead of tenant-run aborts. The same PR notes that `getAllSites` can surface sites the app cannot read; in builds with this fix, those 423 sites should be recorded and skipped rather than blocking the rest of the tenant crawl.

## 4. Throughput bottleneck is mostly SharePoint fetch/permissions, not general compute

Earlier suspicion included CPU embeddings and AWS sizing, but later evidence points strongly to SharePoint retrieval and permission sync. On Apr. 28, only one docfetching pod was busy despite multiple replicas, and engineering explained that one connector’s SharePoint fetch stage runs as a single long-lived task. [[13]](https://onyx-company.slack.com/archives/C097NBWMY8Y/p1777395633493289?thread_ts=1777395633.493289)

## 5. SharePoint API rate limiting is suspected but not proven

There is circumstantial evidence that SharePoint API latency/rate-limit pressure matters, especially given permission-heavy REST/Graph calls, but retrieved records do not show explicit `429 Too Many Requests` errors. Treat as a high-priority hypothesis requiring metrics, not as a proven root cause. [[13]](https://onyx-company.slack.com/archives/C097NBWMY8Y/p1777395633493289?thread_ts=1777395633.493289), [[14]](https://app.fireflies.ai/view/01KQATHEAM3DR2AHS5VKRGAMHF?t=2048.29)

## 6. Deployment/version gaps delayed fixes

Scania moved from `v2.12.6` to `v3.2.1` to `v3.3.0`, while fixes and diagnostics were being identified. Old versions lacked embedding swap, permission sync was not running in `v3.2.1`, local hotfixes were applied in `v3.3.0`, and missing OpenSearch/migration state may block moving to versions with better metrics. [[1]](https://onyx-company.slack.com/archives/C09B4PBPFN2/p1776696156151729?thread_ts=1776696156.151729), [[3]](https://onyx-company.slack.com/archives/C09B4PBPFN2/p1777566141560249?thread_ts=1777564268.604939), [[2]](https://onyx-company.slack.com/archives/C09B4PBPFN2/p1778522482318179?thread_ts=1778522442.236789), [[5]](https://onyx-company.slack.com/archives/C09B4PBPFN2/p1778686355854159?thread_ts=1778686355.854159)

## 7. Scania’s security model and data scale make this a difficult customer environment

Scania’s security model rejects broad `read all`, asks for `site select`, and raises concerns about OneDrive, DLP, sensitivity labels, encrypted files, permission-change lag, and data egress. Scania’s SharePoint estate may be extremely large and decentralized, with related meeting context discussing up to 150 million documents. [[6]](https://onyx-company.slack.com/archives/C09B4PBPFN2/p1772552968781719), [[7]](https://onyx-company.slack.com/archives/C09B4PBPFN2/p1773250716080289), [[14]](https://app.fireflies.ai/view/01KQATHEAM3DR2AHS5VKRGAMHF?t=2048.29)

Unhandled connector-generator exceptions during docfetching still fail the attempt, as do infra, heartbeat, and usage-limit failures.

   - Do not present throttling as proven unless logs show explicit rate-limit evidence. [[13]](https://onyx-company.slack.com/archives/C097NBWMY8Y/p1777395633493289?thread_ts=1777395633.493289), [[14]](https://app.fireflies.ai/view/01KQATHEAM3DR2AHS5VKRGAMHF?t=2048.29)

2. **Explain permission-preserving tradeoffs** — organization-public connectors are faster because they skip document-level permission fetching; permission-synced connectors are safer but slower. [[14]](https://app.fireflies.ai/view/01KQATHEAM3DR2AHS5VKRGAMHF?t=2048.29)
